chunks: "Aliasing is what happens when you sample a signal too slowly: frequencies above half the sample rate don't just disappear, they fold back and show up as lower frequencies in your data, and once that happens you can't tell the alias from a real signal at that lower frequency.
The simplest example: sample a 900 hertz sine at 1000 samples per second. The samples are exactly the same as those of a 100 hertz sine, so the data says 100 hertz.
In general the apparent frequency is the absolute difference between the signal frequency and the nearest multiple of the sample rate.
A 1200 hertz tone sampled at 1000 comes out at 200; 2300 comes out at 300.
You see it in everyday life as the wagon wheel effect in films, where the wheel seems to spin slowly or backwards, and in moiré patterns in images.
In hardware it shows up when, say, a 500 kilohertz buck converter ripple is sampled by a 100 kilosample-per-second ADC: it aliases to DC and looks like a constant offset error.
And also all the broadband noise above the Nyquist frequency folds into your band and raises the noise floor.

The fix is to prevent it before sampling: put an analog low-pass anti-alias filter ahead of the ADC with a corner below half the sample rate, and often oversample so that the filter can be gentle, then decimate digitally.
A quick test for aliasing is to change the sample rate: a real signal stays put, an alias moves."
